adulterate

uh-DUL-tuh-rayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To adulterate is to make impure or weaken the quality of, usually by adding an inferior substance.

Regulators fined the company for adulterating the fruit juice with cheap corn syrup.

Example

Some ancient Roman winemakers were known to adulterate their wine with lead-based sweeteners.

The wine wasn't just weaker -- something inferior and harmful had been mixed into it, which is exactly what adulterate describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

contaminate: To contaminate is to make something impure or unsafe with an unwanted substance — germs, chemicals, a spill — and it is very often accidental. To adulterate is deliberate product fraud: someone mixes a cheaper or inferior filler into a product sold as pure, usually to stretch it for profit.

dilute: To dilute something is to weaken its strength by thinning it, usually with water or another neutral liquid, and there is nothing dishonest about it — you dilute juice or paint on purpose. To adulterate is to debase a product by sneaking in an inferior substance, cheating whoever buys it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cleanse: remove impurities from something

Where it sits · how harmful the tampering becomes — water down → adulterate → poison

water down vs. adulterate: Watering something down just weakens it; adulterating it usually means mixing in something inferior or even harmful.

poison vs. adulterate: Adulterating something makes it lower-quality or impure; poisoning it makes it actively dangerous to consume.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ad-

prefix — ad-: to, toward (Latin)

root — ulter

root — ulter: other (Latin (alter))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or perform an action (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Adulterate comes from Latin ad- ('to') + alter ('other') + -ate -- literally 'to make into something other,' capturing how the original substance is corrupted by a foreign addition.

Use the root in a new word: alter

Use the root in a new word: alter: The same alter root gives us the everyday word alter, 'to make something different,' and alternative, 'another option.'
